content:
Critics argue that the doctrine of abrogation (naskh) lets a later verse of the Quran cancel an earlier one, and that the so-called Sword Verse, 9:5, wipes out the verses on peace. They name "no compulsion in religion" (2:256) and the promise to righteous Jews and Christians (5:69) as two casualties.

Part of this is real. Abrogation is a classical doctrine, and 9:5 does command fighting. Below are five points: what 9:5 says in context, what the theory covers, how far scholars differ on its scope, and how the sources treat 2:256 and 5:69. Each objection is stated at full strength and then answered from the sources.

The verse says "kill the polytheists wherever you find them," and the words are there. Any honest answer starts by conceding that. The dispute is over who is meant, when and under what conditions.

Surah 9 opens by ending the treaties of specific tribes who had broken them, with four months of open travel granted first (9:1-2). Verse 9:4 then exempts those polytheists who kept their agreements and orders that their treaties be honoured to the end of their term. Verse 9:7 spares those bound by a treaty at the Sacred Mosque so long as they stay upright. Verse 9:13 gives the reason for the war: a people who broke their oaths and "began it against you first." Verse 9:5 itself ends by letting go anyone who repents, and 9:6 orders that a polytheist who asks for protection be granted it and escorted to a place of safety.[1] A text that protects treaty-keepers and travelling listeners within the same passage is hard to read as a general order against every unbeliever everywhere.

The setting is recorded in the hadith. The opening of the surah was proclaimed at the pilgrimage of the ninth year after the Hijra, when the Prophet sent Abu Bakr to lead it and Ali to announce the end of the treaties. Abu Hurayra, who was among the announcers, reports that they proclaimed that no polytheist would perform the pilgrimage after that year and that no one would circle the House naked, and that those with a treaty would have it honoured to its term.[2] The verse belongs to a specific announcement about specific treaties, made at a specific time.

The doctrine rests on 2:106: "We do not abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten except that We bring one better than it or similar to it." A related verse, 16:101, speaks of one verse being substituted for another.[3] The critic says this makes the Quran unusable, since any verse might be cancelled without warning.

The classical theory is narrower than that. It applies to legal rulings, and not to reports of events, promises or matters of belief, since a statement of fact cannot be replaced by another. Standard examples are the widow's waiting period of a year in 2:240, replaced by four months and ten days in 2:234, and the change of the direction of prayer in 2:142-144.[4] Jurists required a clear conflict that cannot be harmonised and a known order of revelation. Later writers also observe that the earliest generations used the word naskh loosely, to include qualifying a general rule or limiting an absolute one, and that the later legal theory narrowed it.[5]

Change in revealed law is not unique to the Quran. Muslim scholars pointed out that the Torah itself records changes: Jacob married two sisters, which the later law of Leviticus forbids, and many laws given to Israel replaced earlier practice. The New Testament speaks of the old covenant as obsolete and has Jesus declare all foods clean.[6] Christians and Jews have their own ways of explaining these changes, and abrogation is the Islamic way. Its principle, that God may change a ruling as circumstances and His wisdom require, is shared in some form by all three traditions.

The claim that the Sword Verse cancels over a hundred verses has a source. Some compilers of lists of abrogated verses counted very widely, and 9:5 appears in such lists as the verse that overrides earlier calls to forbearance. A critic who cites this is describing a view that some scholars held.

It was never the only view. Al-Suyuti, in his work on the Quranic sciences, reduced the list to about twenty verses.[7] Shah Waliullah of Delhi reduced it further, to five.[8] Abu Muslim al-Isfahani is reported to have denied that any Quranic ruling is abrogated, and al-Razi discusses his argument when commenting on 2:106.[9] Many of the verses on the long lists are cases where a general rule was qualified or a hard circumstance passed, which the narrower scholars refused to call abrogation. So the figure of 124, given by Hibat Allah ibn Salama, marks one end of a range, and a reader needs to know which scholar is being quoted before accepting that it represents the teaching of Islam.

Modern scholarship has continued the narrowing. Many contemporary scholars hold that very few verses are abrogated in the strict legal sense, and that most apparent conflicts are resolved by reading each verse in its context, with general rules qualified by specific ones.[10] Some argue, following Abu Muslim, that 2:106 refers to the laws of earlier scriptures that the Quran replaced, and not to verses within the Quran. The debate is technical, and it does not support the critic's claim that a single verse cancelled the Quran's teaching on peace.

Verse 2:256 reads: "There is no compulsion in religion; right has become distinct from error."[11] The critic says that 9:5 abrogated it. That view is on record: the commentaries of al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that some early authorities took the verse to be abrogated, and that others restricted it to the People of the Book who accept the protection of the Muslim state.[12] Both works also record the other readings. Al-Tabari himself rejects the claim that the verse was abrogated by the permission to fight, and holds that it protects everyone allowed to keep his religion under the protection of the Muslim state.

The reported occasion of the verse supports the plain reading. Abu Dawud relates that some women of the Ansar, the Medinan helpers, had sons who had been raised as Jews, and the verse came when the families wished to make them Muslims by force.[13] The same principle is stated elsewhere in the Quran: "Would you compel people until they become believers?" (10:99) and "let whoever wishes believe, and let whoever wishes disbelieve" (18:29).[14] Faith is a matter of conviction, and a conversion extracted by force cannot supply it. Verse 9:6, in the same surah as the Sword Verse, protects a polytheist who listens and then leaves unconverted.

The practice of the early state supports the same reading. The Christians and Jews of the conquered lands kept their religion under treaties that guaranteed their churches, synagogues and worship, and the jurists built the law of the dhimma on that practice. If 9:5 had abolished 2:256, those treaties would have made no sense, and the jurists who wrote them knew both verses. The arrangements had their own inequalities, discussed in the article on the jizya, but forced conversion was not part of them.

Verse 5:69 says that those who believe, and the Jews, the Sabians and the Christians, whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does good, will have no fear and will not grieve. Verse 2:62 is close to it in wording.[15] The critic holds that later verses cancelled this promise. Al-Tabari reports a saying attributed to Ibn Abbas that 2:62 was abrogated by 3:85, "whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him."[16] That is a real report, and it shows that a classical position of this kind existed.

Other commentators took the promise as standing. The Quran uses islam for submission to God in the sense that earlier prophets practised it, and it calls Abraham and the disciples of Jesus muslims (3:67, 3:52).[17] On that reading 3:85 does not cancel 5:69; it defines the same condition of faith in God, the Last Day and good conduct. The scholars do differ on whether a person to whom the message of Muhammad has clearly come can rely on this promise. The point here is that the verse was never simply deleted from the Quran's teaching, and the sources preserve a plain disagreement.

The strongest form of the objection is that the existence of the abrogation claim shows that some scholars read the Quran in a harsh way, whatever others said. That is true, and Muslims should know it. The answer is that Islamic law has always been a field of argument, and that the reading of 2:62 and 5:69 as standing has as long a pedigree as the reading of them as abrogated. A critic who quotes only one side of a recorded debate gives only a partial account of what the tradition actually holds.

The bottom line

Abrogation is a genuine classical doctrine, 9:5 does command fighting, and some early commentators did say that it overrode gentler verses. Those points can be conceded. The theory covers legal rulings under strict conditions, scholars have counted the abrogated verses anywhere from none to over a hundred, and 2:256 and 5:69 were read as standing by many commentators.

Verse 9:5 itself sits inside a passage that protects treaty-keepers and safe-conduct seekers. A reader who wants to know what Islam teaches has to ask which scholars said what, and why.

Notes

  1. Quran 9:1-7 and 9:13.
  2. Sahih al-Bukhari 4655, Book of Commentary, on Surat al-Tawba, report of Abu Hurayra; compare no. 369.
  3. Quran 2:106 and 16:101.
  4. Quran 2:234, 2:240 and 2:142-144; the examples are standard in works on the principles of jurisprudence.
  5. Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, vol. 3, p. 344: "what appears from the words of the early scholars is that naskh, in their usage, is broader than in the words of the legal theorists".
  6. Genesis 29:21–30 with Leviticus 18:18; Hebrews 8:13; Mark 7:19.
  7. Hibat Allah ibn Salama, al-Nasikh wa al-Mansukh, p. 46, on the sword verse and 124 verses; al-Suyuti, al-Itqan fi ulum al-Quran, the chapter on the abrogating and the abrogated; on his count and Shah Waliullah's, see "Abrogation in the Qur'an", Deoband.org, November 2010.
  8. Shah Waliullah al-Dihlawi, al-Fawz al-kabir fi usul al-tafsir.
  9. Al-Razi, Mafatih al-ghayb, commentary on Quran 2:106, sixth question: "Abu Muslim ibn Bahr said that it did not occur."
  10. On the modern narrowing of naskh, see Louay Fatoohi, Abrogation in the Qur'an and Islamic Law (New York: Routledge, 2013).
  11. Quran 2:256.
  12. Al-Tabari, Jami al-bayan, commentary on Quran 2:256 (the reports of al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd for abrogation, of Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Abbas against, and his own verdict); Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-azim, on the same verse. Tabari (Dar al-Tarbiya wa-l-Turath edition, Shamela text): commentary on 2:256 opens at vol. 5, p. 407.
  13. Sunan Abi Dawud 2682 (Book of Jihad, chapter on compelling a captive to accept Islam), graded sound by al-Albani.
  14. Quran 10:99 and 18:29.
  15. Quran 5:69 and 2:62.
  16. Al-Tabari, Jami al-bayan, commentary on Quran 2:62, which cites Quran 3:85. Tabari (Dar al-Tarbiya wa-l-Turath edition, Shamela text), vol. 2, p. 155: the report is from Ibn Abbas through Ali ibn Abi Talha, and Tabari prefers the reading that does not treat 2:62 as abrogated.
  17. Quran 3:85, 3:67 and 3:52.
